weeks.title: Auth log anatomy — failures, sources, and the success that follows
weeks.lesson: Ticket SOC-2101 lands at 01:20 on the Night Shift Desk: eight lines from the bastion host's sshd log and a request to say whether anything matters. Read a log line left to right as a sentence. The timestamp says when, the host and process say where, and the message says what happened to whom from which address. In this fixture 203.0.113.45 fails three times as root, 198.51.100.7 tries the made-up accounts admin and oracle twice, and 192.0.2.10 fails once right after the user naiya logged in with her key from the same machine. Counting failures per source is the start, not the finding. The line that changes the night is the last one: Accepted password for root from 203.0.113.45, seconds after that address failed. A success that follows a run of failures from the same source is the pattern analysts escalate, because it can mean a guessed password. Naiya's typo after a good key login is noise you note and move past. All addresses here come from documentation ranges, so nobody's real server appears in the course, and you never paste a live customer log into a chat tool to save time.
weeks.worked_example: 203.0.113.45 failed 3×, 198.51.100.7 failed 2×, 192.0.2.10 failed 1×; Accepted password for root from 203.0.113.45 at 01:15:31 → escalate
weeks.assignment: Submit lab_soc_log_parse JSON for SOC-2101: failed_by_ip, top_source, accepted_after_failures.

weeks.title: Windowed detection — a threshold means nothing without a clock
weeks.lesson: SOC-2202 asks you to turn last night's eyeballing into a rule the SIEM can run. 'Four failed logins' is not a rule until you say within how long. The fixture lists eleven failures with second offsets. With a threshold of four inside a sixty-second sliding window, 203.0.113.45 fires at second 70: the failures at 20, 50, 65 and 70 all sit within sixty seconds of each other, while the first one at second 0 has already aged out. 198.51.100.7 never fires, because its attempts at 200, 230, 250 and 265 span sixty-five seconds, one heartbeat too slow. Widen the window to ninety seconds and that address alerts at 265 as well. Neither choice is free. A wider window catches slow guessing and also pulls in people who mistype their passwords on a cold morning. Write the threshold and window into the rule's description so the next analyst can reason about a miss, and replay the rule against stored events before you switch it on. The lab grader replays your parameters, so it rejects an alert list that would only be true for a different window.
weeks.worked_example: threshold 4 in 60 s → 203.0.113.45 fires at t=70 (events 20, 50, 65, 70); 198.51.100.7 does not; widen to 90 s → it fires at 265
weeks.assignment: Submit lab_soc_window_rule JSON for SOC-2202: threshold, window_s, and the alerts your rule fires.

choices: More false positives from ordinary typos

weeks.title: Detection quality — precision, recall, and the analyst's hour
weeks.lesson: SOC-2303 is a NO_AI week: do the fractions on paper and show each line, because these four numbers decide whether a rule stays on. A month of the brute-force rule produced 60 alerts. Eighteen were real attacks, true positives, and forty-two were not, false positives. Six real attacks slipped through without an alert, false negatives, and 934 quiet events were correctly left alone. Precision asks how often an alert is worth opening: 18 out of 60, or 0.30. Recall asks how many real attacks the rule caught: 18 out of 24, or 0.75. The false-positive rate compares wrong alerts with all benign events, 42 out of 976, about 0.043, which sounds tiny and still costs forty-two investigations. At ten minutes each that is seven analyst-hours spent proving nothing happened. A precision under one half means most alerts are noise, so the honest call is needs tuning, not 'the rule works'. Tuning that raises precision often lowers recall, so record both before and after a change, and never report recall alone because it flatters a noisy rule.
weeks.worked_example: TP 18, FP 42, FN 6, TN 934 → precision 18/60 = 0.30, recall 18/24 = 0.75, FPR 42/976 = 0.043 → needs tuning
weeks.assignment: Submit lab_soc_detection_metrics JSON for SOC-2303 (NO_AI): precision, recall, false_positive_rate, alerts, needs_tuning.

weeks.title: Indicator hygiene — hash it, defang it, then compare
weeks.lesson: SOC-2404 arrives with a suspicious attachment name and a link from a user report. Indicators of compromise are only useful if you can compare them exactly and pass them around safely. For files that means a cryptographic hash: SHA-256 turns any sequence of bytes into a 64-character fingerprint, and a single changed byte produces an unrelated digest, so the lab recomputes the hash from the inert sample text instead of trusting a pasted value. For links it means defanging before the indicator goes into a ticket, chat, or report: write hxxp instead of http and bracket every dot in the host, so update-check.example.net becomes update-check[.]example[.]net and nobody's mail client turns it into a clickable trap. Only after both steps do you check the desk's indicator list. Here the sample hash and the domain are both on it, so the answer is a match and the ticket goes to the phishing playbook. A miss does not mean safe, it means unknown, and the course's sample is inert text, never real malware, so nobody downloads or detonates anything on a personal laptop.
weeks.worked_example: sha256('WAIKE-SOC training sample: …') = fc6c0f88…e657; http://update-check.example.net/payload → hxxp://update-check[.]example[.]net/payload; on IOC list → match
weeks.assignment: Submit lab_soc_ioc_match JSON for SOC-2404: sample_text, sha256, url, defanged_url, ioc_match.

weeks.title: ATT&CK mapping — describe behaviour, not villains
weeks.lesson: SOC-2505 gives the desk five behaviours seen this week and asks for a shared vocabulary. MITRE ATT&CK is a public catalogue of attacker techniques, each with an ID and one or more tactics that say what the attacker was trying to achieve. Many failed SSH logins from one address are T1110, Brute Force, under credential access. A never-before-seen account logging in at three in the morning with a correct password is T1078, Valid Accounts, which ATT&CK lists under several tactics because stolen credentials help an intruder get in, stay in, and blend in. A spoofed invoice attachment is T1566, Phishing, under initial access. PowerShell launched with an encoded command line is T1059, Command and Scripting Interpreter, under execution, and files renamed with a .locked suffix beside a ransom note are T1486, Data Encrypted for Impact. Mapping lets the day shift, the detection engineers, and management talk about the same thing. It does not tell you who did it. Plenty of groups use the same techniques, so the lab requires actor_attribution_claim to stay false.
weeks.worked_example: B1 brute force → T1110 credential_access; B3 spoofed invoice → T1566 initial_access; B5 .locked files → T1486 impact; actor_attribution_claim false
weeks.assignment: Submit lab_soc_attack_map JSON for SOC-2505: technique ID and tactic for B1–B5, actor_attribution_claim false.

choices: Stolen credentials help an intruder enter, persist, and evade

weeks.title: Email authentication — passing is not the same as aligned
weeks.lesson: SOC-2606 compares two invoices that both claim to come from Harbor Pay. SPF checks whether the sending server is allowed to send for the envelope's return-path domain. DKIM checks a signature made with a key published by the domain in the signature's d= tag. Both can pass for a domain that has nothing to do with the address the reader sees in the From line. DMARC closes that gap with alignment: at least one passing check must belong to the same organisational domain as the visible From address. Under relaxed alignment, subdomains count, so in message A the From address mail.harborpay.example, the return path bounce.harborpay.example, and the DKIM domain harborpay.example all share harborpay.example, and DMARC passes. Message B also shows SPF pass and DKIM pass, but both checks vouch for bulk-sender.example while the From line says harborpay.example, so DMARC fails. That is exactly the shape of a convincing spoof, and a user who sees 'SPF pass' in a header viewer will be fooled unless someone on the desk explains alignment.
weeks.worked_example: A: From mail.harborpay.example, SPF via bounce.harborpay.example, DKIM d=harborpay.example → aligned → DMARC pass; B: From harborpay.example, SPF/DKIM pass for bulk-sender.example → not aligned → DMARC fail

weeks.title: CVSS v3.1 by hand — from vector string to severity band
weeks.lesson: SOC-2707 is the second NO_AI week, because a desk that only reads scores off a website cannot defend them in a patch meeting. The FIRST CVSS v3.1 base score turns eight metrics into a number. Impact starts from the confidentiality, integrity, and availability weights, 0.56 for High, 0.22 for Low, 0 for None, combined as ISS = 1 − (1 − C)(1 − I)(1 − A). For an unchanged scope, impact is 6.42 × ISS. Exploitability is 8.22 × attack vector × attack complexity × privileges required × user interaction, where a network vector weighs 0.85 and low complexity 0.77. For the familiar AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H vector, ISS is about 0.9148, impact about 5.873, exploitability about 3.887, and their sum rounds up to 9.8, Critical. Roundup means the next tenth upward, not the nearest, which is where hand scorers slip. A local, low-privilege flaw that only leaks data, AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N, lands at 5.5, Medium. The base score describes the flaw, not your network; asset value enters next week.
weeks.worked_example: AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H → ISS 0.9148, impact 5.873, exploitability 3.887 → Roundup 9.8 Critical; AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N → 5.5 Medium
weeks.assignment: Submit lab_soc_cvss_score JSON for SOC-2707 (NO_AI): at least two vectors with base_score and severity.

weeks.title: Triage queue — severity meets asset criticality
weeks.lesson: SOC-2808 hands you six open alerts at once and one pair of hands. Severity alone is a poor sort key, because a critical alert on a lobby kiosk can matter less than a high alert on the domain controller. The desk multiplies a severity weight, four for critical down to one for low, by the asset's criticality from one to three. A5, critical on a criticality-three server, scores twelve and goes first. A1, high on criticality three, scores nine. A3 and A6 both score six, so the earlier arrival, A3 at minute two, goes ahead of A6 at minute eight. A2, the critical alert on a criticality-one kiosk, scores four, and A4 scores three. Each alert also gets a due time: the minute it arrived plus the service-level target for its severity, fifteen minutes for critical, an hour for high, four hours for medium, a day for low. That puts A2's due time at minute 27 even though it sits fifth in the queue, which is a signal to ask for help rather than quietly breach the target. A queue is a plan you can explain to the shift lead, not a mood.
weeks.worked_example: priority = severity weight × criticality: A5 12, A1 9, A3 6 (t=2), A6 6 (t=8), A2 4, A4 3; due = received + SLA (critical 15, high 60, medium 240, low 1440)

weeks.title: Shift metrics — MTTD, MTTR, and the median that resists one bad night
weeks.lesson: SOC-2909 asks how the week went, in numbers management will read. Mean time to detect is the average gap between when something happened and when the desk noticed. The four incidents took 12, 45, 5 and 70 minutes to detect, so MTTD is 33 minutes. Mean time to resolve, measured here from detection to resolution, averages 78, 65, 35 and 150 minutes to 82. Define the start and end points in the report, because some teams measure resolution from occurrence and their numbers are not comparable with yours. One slow detection, the seventy-minute ransomware case, pulls the mean up; the median of the four detection times is 28.5 minutes and tells a steadier story about a typical night. Report both, and name the outlier instead of hiding it, since that is the incident the next tuning effort should study. Four incidents are a tiny sample. A dashboard that celebrates a five-minute drop in MTTD between two such weeks is reporting noise, so the course asks for the numbers and a sentence about how much they can bear.
weeks.worked_example: time to detect = 12, 45, 5, 70 min → MTTD 33, median 28.5; time to resolve from detection = 78, 65, 35, 150 → MTTR 82
weeks.assignment: Submit lab_soc_shift_metrics JSON for SOC-2909: mttd_min, mttr_min, median_ttd_min.

weeks.title: Shift handoff — open incidents, NIST phases, and clean boundaries
weeks.lesson: SOC-2A10 closes the night. A handoff is the document the day shift reads with its first coffee, so it must be complete without you in the room. List every open incident with its ATT&CK technique ID, the NIST SP 800-61 phase it is in, and a named next owner. The phases are preparation, detection and analysis, containment with eradication and recovery, and post-incident activity; saying 'containment' tells the reader which actions are already done and which are waiting. Carry the shift's MTTD and MTTR from last week's calculation rather than rounding them in your head, and say what changed in the rules you tuned. Two boundaries close every Night Shift Desk packet. It contains no real customer data, only the course's synthetic logs and documentation addresses, and it contains no offensive tooling: the desk detects, contains, and documents; it does not build exploits or scan systems it does not own. Mentors check the packet against six or more passed labs and ask you to walk one incident from first log line to current phase out loud.

DIGITAL_CONFIDENCE.kinesthetic_hook: Ten Library Lab help-desk cards: find the file → read the drive label → judge a password → read a link → build a budget sheet → measure typing → fit an attachment → plan backups → check screen contrast → write a safety plan.

weeks.title: Folders and paths — knowing where a file really lives
weeks.lesson: Help card DCO-3101: Ana saved a summer photo and the file dialog now says 'not found'. Every file has an address called a path, written from the top of the drive down through folders, like /home/ana/Documents/photos/summer.jpg. That full form is an absolute path because it starts at the root, the single slash. Programs also accept relative paths that start from wherever you are standing, called the current working directory. Two dots mean the folder above, and a single dot means here. Standing in /home/ana/Documents/letters, the relative path ../photos/2026/../summer.jpg climbs out of letters into Documents, steps into photos and into 2026, then climbs back out of 2026, landing on /home/ana/Documents/photos/summer.jpg. Walk it with your finger on a drawn tree before trusting it. Windows writes C:\Users\Ana\Documents with backslashes and a drive letter, but the idea of climbing and descending is the same. When a file goes missing, ask two questions out loud: where am I standing, and which way does the path walk from here.
weeks.worked_example: cwd /home/ana/Documents/letters + ../photos/2026/../summer.jpg → /home/ana/Documents/photos/summer.jpg
weeks.assignment: Submit lab_dco_paths JSON for DCO-3101: two tasks with cwd, relative path, and resolved absolute path.

weeks.title: Storage units — why a 500 GB drive shows 465 GiB
weeks.lesson: DCO-3202 is a NO_AI week; work the division on paper. A patron bought a '500 GB' drive and thinks the store cheated her because the computer shows about 465 GB. Nobody cheated. Drive makers count in powers of ten, so a gigabyte is 1,000,000,000 bytes. Many operating systems count in powers of two, where a gibibyte, GiB, is 1,073,741,824 bytes, and then label the result GB anyway. Divide 500,000,000,000 by 1,073,741,824 and you get about 465.66, the same drive described in a bigger unit. The same confusion bites when deciding whether something will fit. Her phone holds 1,200 photos at about 4.2 MB each, where MB means a million bytes, so the folder is 5.04 billion bytes. In the binary unit that is about 4.69 GiB, and the laptop says 4.5 GiB free. It will not fit, even though '5 GB into 4.5' felt close. Write the unit beside every number, convert both sides to the same unit before comparing, and leave room to spare, because a completely full disk makes most computers slow and unstable.
weeks.worked_example: 500 GB = 500×10^9 B = 465.66 GiB; 1,200 photos × 4.2 MB = 5.04×10^9 B = 4.694 GiB > 4.5 GiB free → does not fit

weeks.title: Passwords and passphrases — strength is length times choice
weeks.lesson: DCO-3303 starts with a sticky note that says P@ssw0rd! and a question: is this strong? Strength depends on how the password was chosen, not on how it looks. If every character is picked at random from a pool, the number of possibilities is the pool size raised to the length, and we measure it in bits: length times log2 of the pool. Four words drawn at random from a 7,776-word dice list give about 51.7 bits. Eight characters drawn at random from the 95 printable keyboard symbols give about 52.6 bits. Twelve random lowercase letters give about 56.4 bits, stronger than either, because length grows strength faster than adding symbols. P@ssw0rd! scores far lower than its nine characters suggest, because guessing tools try dictionary words with common swaps first. The NIST digital identity guidance, SP 800-63B, favours long memorable secrets, checking them against lists of known-breached passwords, and changing them when there is evidence of compromise rather than on a fixed calendar. Use a different secret on every site, and let a password manager remember them.

weeks.title: Reading a link — the real address is at the right end
weeks.lesson: DCO-3404 is a text message that says a bank account is locked and offers a link. Before tapping, read the address the way a computer does. Skip the https:// and stop at the first single slash after it; what sits between is the hostname. Read the hostname from the right end, label by label, because the rightmost labels say who owns it. In https://account.harborbank.example.verify-login.example.net/session the hostname is account.harborbank.example.verify-login.example.net, and its last two labels are example.net. The bank's name near the left is just decoration chosen by whoever owns example.net, which is not the bank. So the call is: do not open. Real organisations rarely ask you to log in from a message; type the bank's address yourself or use its app. Some country endings use three labels, such as .co.uk, so the rule 'last two labels' is a starting point, and the course's examples use the reserved .example endings so nobody is sent anywhere real. When unsure, show the message to the library desk rather than replying.

weeks.title: Spreadsheet formulas — let the sheet do the arithmetic
weeks.lesson: DCO-3505 is a monthly budget written on the back of an envelope that never adds up the same way twice. Move it into a spreadsheet: labels in column A, amounts in column B, one row per item. Rent is 650, food 240, the bus pass 55, the phone 35, and savings 120. Instead of typing the total, write =SUM(B2:B6) and the sheet answers 1,100, then keeps answering correctly when the phone bill changes. =AVERAGE(B2:B6) gives 220, the typical line, and =MAX(B2:B6) finds the largest amount, which belongs to rent. To see how much of the month food takes, divide its cell by the total cell, =B3/B7, and format the result as a percentage: about 21.82 percent. The habit worth keeping is that numbers you typed live in one place and every other number is a formula pointing at them. A total typed by hand goes stale the first time anything changes, and that is how budgets quietly stop matching reality. Save the file somewhere you will find it, with a name that says what and when.

weeks.title: Keyboard fluency — gross speed, net speed, accuracy
weeks.lesson: DCO-3606 is a NO_AI week because it measures your own hands. Job applications and online forms reward people who can type steadily, so the library runs a five-minute practice passage. Typing speed is counted in words per minute, where a 'word' is defined as five characters, spaces included, so long and short words count fairly. Typing 1,250 characters in five minutes is 250 'words' over five minutes, a gross speed of 50 WPM. Mistakes left uncorrected are subtracted per minute: fifteen errors over five minutes costs three, so net speed is 47 WPM. Accuracy compares correct characters with all characters, 1,235 out of 1,250, or 98.8 percent. Most learners improve fastest by slowing down until accuracy stays near ninety-eight percent, then letting speed return, because unlearning a mistyped pattern takes longer than learning it right. Sit square to the keyboard, keep wrists level, and rest the index fingers on the small bumps on F and J. Record the three numbers each week rather than chasing a single best run.

weeks.title: Attachments — why a 19 MB file will not fit under 25 MB
weeks.lesson: DCO-3707: a patron's resume portfolio is 19 MB, the mail service says attachments up to 25 MB, and sending still fails. Email was designed to carry text, so attachments are converted into text with an encoding called base64 before they travel. Base64 turns every three bytes into four characters, so the encoded file is about a third larger: four times the byte count divided by three, rounded up to a whole group. Nineteen million bytes become 25,333,336 bytes, just over the 25,000,000-byte limit, which is why the message bounces even though the file looked small enough. An 18 MB file would encode to 24,000,000 bytes and squeak through. When something will not fit, do not split it into a dozen emails or squeeze the quality until the pictures blur. Upload it to a storage service, share a link with view-only permission, and mention in the message what the link is and how long it will stay up. Never attach other people's personal documents to practice messages; the lab uses only made-up byte counts.

weeks.title: Backups — three copies, two kinds of storage, one away from home
weeks.lesson: DCO-3808 begins with tears: a laptop died and took two years of family photos with it. A simple rule, called 3-2-1, prevents most of these stories. Keep three copies of anything you would miss, the original plus two backups. Store them on at least two different kinds of storage, so one failure type, such as a batch of bad drives, cannot take everything. Keep one copy somewhere else, away from the house, so a fire, flood, or theft leaves something behind. The library's example plan has the photos on the laptop's SSD, a copy on a USB hard drive at home, and a copy in a cloud folder; that is three copies, three kinds of storage, and one offsite. There is a fourth rule people forget: a backup you have never restored is a hope, not a plan. Once a month, pick a random file and open it from each backup. Two copies on the same USB stick are one copy with extra steps, and a sync folder that mirrors deletions instantly is convenient but is not a backup on its own.

weeks.title: Readable screens — measuring colour contrast
weeks.lesson: DCO-3909: the library's new event flyer uses pale grey text, and a patron with low vision cannot read it. Readability can be measured. The W3C's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, WCAG 2.2, define a contrast ratio between text and background colours. Each colour's red, green, and blue values are converted to a relative luminance, a weighted brightness in which green counts most and blue least, and the ratio is the lighter luminance plus 0.05 divided by the darker luminance plus 0.05. Black on white is 21 to 1; identical colours are 1 to 1. Normal-size text needs at least 4.5 to 1 for level AA, and large text needs 3 to 1. The grey #767676 on white measures about 4.54 and just passes. One step lighter, #777777, measures about 4.48 and fails for normal text, even though most eyes cannot tell the two apart, which is exactly why you measure rather than guess. Use a contrast checker before printing or posting, and remember contrast is one accessibility check among many, not the whole job.

weeks.lesson: DCO-3A10 asks each learner to leave the Library Lab with one page they will actually use. It names a password manager, because unique secrets for every site are impossible to remember otherwise. It turns on multi-factor sign-in for the email account first, since email is where every other password reset arrives, so whoever controls it controls the rest. It lists the backup copies by media and location, passes the 3-2-1 rule, and records the date of the last test restore. It names a real person or desk to show strange messages to, such as the library's IT desk, so nobody has to judge a convincing scam alone at midnight. It records which colours and font sizes work for the reader's eyes. It never contains an actual password, PIN, or recovery code; those belong in the manager or on paper locked away, not on a page that might be photographed. weeks.title: Power supply budget — parts, headroom, and the smallest adequate unit
weeks.lesson: Work order ISH-4101: a donated tower is getting a graphics card so a youth club can edit video, and the old 450 W power supply is suspect. Start with a parts list and each part's rated draw from its spec sheet, not from a forum guess. The processor is rated 125 W, the card 200 W, the motherboard about 50, two memory sticks about 10 together, the SSD about 8, and the fans about 12, for 405 W. A supply running near its limit gets hot, loud, and less efficient, and real loads spike above their averages, so the bench adds a quarter on top: 405 × 1.25 is 506.25 W. The smallest catalogue unit that covers it is 550 W, so the 450 W supply goes in the parts bin. Bigger is not automatically better, since a 1,000 W unit idling at 60 W wastes money and often efficiency. Check that the new supply has the right connectors for the card, and never open a supply's case; the capacitors inside can hold a dangerous charge long after it is unplugged.

weeks.title: Memory channels — the slots you choose set the bandwidth
weeks.lesson: ISH-4202 is a slow machine that has two good memory sticks in it. Desktop boards usually have two memory channels, labelled A and B, each a separate 64-bit path to the processor. Each transfer moves eight bytes per channel, so peak bandwidth in gigabytes per second is the transfer rate in megatransfers per second times eight times the number of channels, divided by a thousand. DDR4-3200 in one channel gives 25.6 GB/s; spread across both channels it gives 51.2. The previous volunteer pushed both sticks into A1 and A2, which sit on the same channel, so the machine runs single-channel and integrated graphics, which borrow system memory, crawl. Moving one stick to B2 doubles the path without buying anything. The board manual names the preferred slots, often A2 and B2 for two sticks, and the firmware setup screen confirms the mode after a reboot. Handle sticks by the edges, match the notch to the key in the slot, and press until both latches click; a half-seated stick is a classic cause of beeps and no display.

weeks.title: RAID — usable space, tolerated failures, and why it is not a backup
weeks.lesson: ISH-4303 is a NO_AI week; build the table by hand. A community centre wants its donated four-bay storage box set up for shared files, with four 4 TB disks. RAID combines disks into one volume with different trade-offs. RAID 0 stripes data across all four for 16 TB and speed, but any single failure loses everything. RAID 1 mirrors the same data on every disk: only 4 TB usable, yet three disks can die. RAID 5 spreads one disk's worth of parity, leaving 12 TB and surviving one failure. RAID 6 uses two disks' worth of parity for 8 TB and survives any two. RAID 10 mirrors pairs and stripes across them, also 8 TB; it is guaranteed to survive one failure and survives a second only if it hits the other pair, so the honest table says one. With large disks, rebuilding after a failure takes many hours and stresses the survivors, which is why RAID 6 suits this box better than RAID 5. Most important: RAID protects against a disk dying, not against deletion, ransomware, or fire, because those damage every copy at once. The centre still needs the 3-2-1 backup plan.

weeks.title: MBR or GPT — the two-terabyte ceiling and UEFI boot
weeks.lesson: ISH-4404 is a new 4 TB data disk that shows only about 2 TB of usable space after the last technician set it up. A disk's partition table records where each partition starts and ends. The older Master Boot Record format stores those positions as 32-bit sector numbers, so it can address at most 2^32 sectors. With the common 512-byte sectors that is 2,199,023,255,552 bytes, two tebibytes, and anything beyond is simply unreachable. The GUID Partition Table uses 64-bit addresses, supports far larger disks, keeps a backup copy of the table at the end of the disk, and allows many more partitions. A 4,000,000,000,000-byte disk is larger than the MBR ceiling, so it must be GPT. Disks with 4,096-byte native sectors stretch MBR to 16 TiB, but they are not what the bench usually sees. To boot an operating system from a GPT disk, the PC's firmware needs to run in UEFI mode rather than legacy BIOS mode, a setting in the firmware setup screen. Converting the scheme erases the table, so copy the data off and confirm the backup before you touch it.

weeks.title: Fault isolation — symptom first, subsystem second, parts last
weeks.lesson: ISH-4505 is five machines on the bench at once and a temptation to start swapping motherboards. Good technicians follow the power-on sequence, because each stage that succeeds rules out everything before it. No lights and no fans means the power path: the outlet, the cable, the supply's rear switch, then the supply itself. Fans spinning with beeps and no picture means the board is alive but the self-test failed, most often memory or a processor that is not seated; reseat the sticks one at a time before anything else. A self-test that passes and then complains there is no boot device points at the boot order in the firmware or a disk that is not detected. A machine that boots and then shows a stop error usually blames the last driver or update installed. Random shutdowns only under heavy load suggest heat or an undersized supply, so check temperatures and last week's power budget. Write down the symptom in the customer's words, the stage it fails at, and the cheapest test that would confirm your guess. Replacing parts before isolating the fault costs money and hides the real cause.

weeks.title: Display bandwidth — will the cable carry the mode?
weeks.lesson: ISH-4606: a donated 4K monitor flickers or drops to 30 Hz on a refurbished PC. A screen mode is a stream of pixels, and the cable has a ceiling. Multiply width by height by refresh rate by bits per pixel: 3,840 by 2,160 at 60 Hz with 24-bit colour is about 11.94 gigabits per second. That ignores the blanking intervals between lines and frames, so the true need is somewhat higher, and the honest label is lower bound. Compare it with each link's usable data rate after encoding overhead: HDMI 1.4 carries about 8.16, HDMI 2.0 about 14.4, and DisplayPort 1.4 about 25.92. The 4K 60 Hz mode fits HDMI 2.0 and DisplayPort 1.4 but not HDMI 1.4, which is why the old port falls back to 30 Hz. Double the refresh to 120 Hz and the need becomes about 23.89 Gbit/s, which only DisplayPort 1.4 carries uncompressed here. Cables and ports are both links in the chain: a certified high-speed cable on an old port still runs at the old port's speed, so read both before promising a customer a mode.

weeks.title: UPS runtime — watt-hours, inverter loss, and a graceful shutdown
weeks.lesson: ISH-4707: the community centre's storage box and router should ride out short power cuts and shut down cleanly during long ones. A battery's energy is in watt-hours, and the uninterruptible power supply converts it back to mains power through an inverter that loses some energy as heat. This unit holds two 12 V, 36 Ah batteries, about 864 Wh, and its inverter is about 85 percent efficient. The load measured at the wall is 300 W, so the runtime is 864 × 0.85 ÷ 300 hours, about 2.45 hours or 146.9 minutes. Batteries age, cold rooms reduce capacity, and the last minutes of a discharge are not reliable, so the bench starts a graceful shutdown no later than 80 percent of the computed runtime; here the plan picks 110 minutes. Configure the storage box to listen for the UPS's low-battery signal over USB or the network, and test it by pulling the plug while someone watches. Never plug a laser printer or a space heater into the battery outlets; their surges can overload the inverter.

weeks.title: Imaging a lab — unicast one by one versus one multicast stream
weeks.lesson: ISH-4808: forty refurbished laptops need the same 32 GB system image before the library's coding club opens. Image sizes are in bytes and network links in bits, so start by multiplying by eight: 256 gigabits per copy. On a gigabit link that really delivers about 70 percent of its rating, one copy takes about 366 seconds, a little over six minutes. Sending the image to each laptop separately, unicast, repeats that forty times through the same server port: about 244 minutes, more than four hours. Multicast sends one stream that every listening machine receives together, so in the ideal case the whole lab finishes in about the time of a single copy, roughly six minutes. Real networks need switches that handle multicast properly, and one slow or faulty laptop can hold the session back, so plan a fallback to unicast for stragglers. Whatever the method, check one finished machine against a list of expected settings before releasing the rest, and record which image version went onto which serial numbers.

weeks.title: Media sanitization — Clear, Purge, or Destroy before a device leaves
weeks.lesson: ISH-4909 is the second NO_AI week, because a sanitization decision has to be yours. Donated machines arrive full of strangers' lives, and the bench's promise is that nothing leaves with them. NIST Special Publication 800-88 frames the choice with three words. Clear uses ordinary commands to overwrite user-addressable storage, enough when the device stays inside the organisation. Purge uses methods that defeat laboratory recovery, such as the drive's own secure-erase or cryptographic-erase commands, and is the floor when a device leaves your control through donation, sale, or a returned lease. Destroy means the media cannot be reused: shredding, disintegrating, or incinerating, and it is the only answer for a drive that has failed and will not accept commands. Solid-state drives remap blocks behind the scenes, so overwriting the visible space can leave old data in spare areas; rely on the drive's purge commands. Every decision ends with verification and a certificate recording the serial number, method, date, and who did it. A quick format is none of the three.

weeks.title: Fiber latency budget — light is slower in glass
weeks.lesson: Change request NIF-5101 asks whether a new 1,145 km fiber route between two regional exchanges can promise game servers a one-way delay under six milliseconds. Light in a vacuum covers about 299,792 km each second, but glass slows it by the fiber's group index, about 1.468, so the signal moves at roughly 204,000 km/s. Divide the route length by that speed: 1,145 km takes about 5.6067 milliseconds. That is propagation, and no upgrade fixes it short of a straighter path. Serialization is the time to clock a packet's bits onto the wire: 1,500 bytes is 12,000 bits, which takes 0.012 ms at one gigabit per second and would take ten times longer on a 100-megabit link. Add them for a one-way floor of about 5.619 ms, before any queueing or equipment delay. Route length is not the straight-line distance on a map; cables follow railways and roads, so ask for the measured route. Using the vacuum speed understates delay by about a third and leads to promises the backbone cannot keep.

weeks.title: IPv6 text and prefixes — one canonical way to write an address
weeks.lesson: NIF-5202 began as an outage: two engineers searched the change log for the same router address and missed each other because they had typed it differently. IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hex digits, and RFC 5952 sets one canonical text form so tools and people agree. Write hex in lowercase, drop leading zeros in each group, and replace the longest run of two or more all-zero groups with a double colon, choosing the first run if two are equally long. A single zero group stays as 0. So 2001:0DB8:0000:0000:0001:0000:0000:0001 has two runs of two zero groups; the first one collapses and the result is 2001:db8::1:0:0:1. The 2001:db8::/32 block is reserved for documentation, which is why this course uses it. Prefix math is about counting bits: a site receives a /48, and LAN segments are /64, so 64 minus 48 leaves 16 bits for subnet numbers, which is 65,536 subnets. Never squeeze a LAN smaller than /64; address autoconfiguration expects it.

weeks.title: Bandwidth-delay product — why one connection cannot fill the pipe
weeks.lesson: NIF-5303: a research group pays for a one-gigabit link to a partner 80 milliseconds away and complains that a single file transfer crawls at a few megabits. TCP may only have one window of unacknowledged bytes in flight, then must wait for acknowledgements to return. The bandwidth-delay product says how many bytes the pipe holds: one gigabit per second times 0.08 seconds is 80 million bits, or 10,000,000 bytes. The original TCP header allows a window of at most 65,535 bytes, so the sender stalls after 64 KiB each round trip; throughput is window times eight divided by the round-trip time, about 6.55 Mbit/s here, less than one percent of the link. RFC 7323 window scaling shifts the advertised window left by a negotiated count; a shift of 8 multiplies 65,535 by 256 to about 16.8 MB, enough to cover the 10 MB product. The fix is end-host tuning and checking that no middlebox strips the option, not buying a bigger link.
weeks.worked_example: 1 Gbit/s × 0.080 s / 8 = 10,000,000 B BDP; 65,535-byte window × 8 / 0.080 s = 6.55 Mbit/s; window scale shift 8 (65,535 × 256 ≥ 10 MB)

weeks.title: BGP best path — policy first, then the shorter story
weeks.lesson: NIF-5404 asks why traffic to a partner network leaves through the long transit path instead of the direct one. Border Gateway Protocol routers hear several routes to the same prefix and pick one by walking an ordered list of attributes, stopping at the first that differs. This course uses a simplified order: highest local preference, shortest AS_PATH, lowest origin code with IGP before EGP before incomplete, lowest MED, then lowest router ID. Local preference is the operator's own policy, so it outranks everything about the route's length. Here R1 offers a one-hop path through documentation AS 64500 but carries local preference 100, while R2 and R3 both carry 200, so R1 is out at the first step even though its path is shortest. R2 and R3 each have four AS numbers, a tie, so the origin decides: R2 is IGP and R3 is EGP, and R2 wins. The deciding attribute is origin. Real routers add steps such as weight and eBGP-over-iBGP; RFC 4271 is the reference, and vendor documents list their full order.

weeks.title: DNS TTL — planning a change the world sees late
weeks.lesson: NIF-5505 is a cutover: a public website moves to new servers at t = 5,000 seconds and the old servers will be switched off soon after. Resolvers that looked up the name keep the answer for its time to live, and RFC 1034 lets them reuse it without asking again. A resolver that cached the record at t = 3,000 with a TTL of 3,600 seconds will hand out the old address until t = 6,600, so its users see the old site for 1,600 seconds after the change. In the worst case a resolver caches the old answer one second before the change and stays stale for the whole TTL, 3,600 seconds. The fix is planning: lower the TTL to something short, such as 300 seconds, at least one old TTL before the change, so by t = 1,400 at the latest, and raise it again once the new servers are stable. Keep the old servers answering until the worst-case window has passed. A change is not live when the zone file is saved; it is live when the last cache has expired.
weeks.worked_example: TTL 3600; resolver cached at t=3000 → expires 6600; record changed at 5000 → stale window 1600 s; worst case 3600 s; lower TTL by t=1400

weeks.title: CDN offload — the miss ratio is what the origin pays for
weeks.lesson: NIF-5606: a public broadcaster expects 12,000 requests per second for a live results page, each object about 150 kilobytes, and its origin servers sit behind a two-gigabit link. A content delivery network answers from edge caches when it can, and only the misses travel back to the origin. The origin's load scales with the miss ratio, one minus the hit ratio. At a 92 percent hit ratio, 8 percent of 12,000 is 960 requests per second, and 960 times 150,000 bytes times 8 bits is 1.152 gigabits per second, uncomfortably close to the two-gigabit link. Raising the hit ratio to 96 percent halves the misses to 480 requests per second and 0.576 Gbit/s. Four points of hit ratio halved the origin's work, which is why cache keys, longer TTLs for static images, and stripping needless query strings matter. The edge still delivers all 14.4 Gbit/s to viewers, so the CDN contract must cover that. Multiplying by the hit ratio instead of the miss ratio gives a number that looks impressive and is wrong.
weeks.worked_example: 12,000 rps × 150 KB: hit 0.92 → 960 rps, 1.152 Gbit/s at origin; hit 0.96 → 480 rps, 0.576 Gbit/s; edge serves 14.4 Gbit/s total

weeks.title: Optical link budget — loss, margin, and the 3 dB rule
weeks.lesson: NIF-5707 is a NO_AI week: do the decibel arithmetic on paper first. A field team must confirm that optics with a 0 dBm transmitter and a receiver sensitivity of −23 dBm will work over a new 40 km span. Decibels add, which is why engineers like them. The planning coefficients are 0.35 dB per kilometre of fiber, 0.5 dB for each mated connector, and 0.1 dB for each fusion splice. Forty kilometres costs 14 dB, four connectors cost 2, and six splices cost 0.6, for 16.6 dB in total. The light arrives at −16.6 dBm, and the receiver can still read it down to −23, so the margin is 6.4 dB. The backbone rule asks for at least 3 dB of margin to cover ageing, dirty connectors, temperature, and the repair splices a backhoe will eventually require, so this span passes. Counting only fiber loss would claim 9 dB of margin and hide two decibels of connectors. Clean and inspect every connector before measuring, and compare the light meter's reading with the budget.

weeks.title: Availability — redundancy in parallel, single points in series
weeks.lesson: NIF-5808: a regional exchange's design has two core routers sharing traffic, each available 99.9 percent of the time, followed by one power feed at 99.95 percent and one fiber uplink at 99.99 percent. The question from management is how many minutes a year customers should expect to lose. A redundant pair fails only when both members are down at once, so its unavailability is the product of theirs: 0.001 times 0.001 is one in a million, making the pair 0.999999 available, assuming failures are independent. Parts in series all have to work, so their availabilities multiply: 0.999999 times 0.9995 times 0.9999 is about 0.9993991. A year has 525,600 minutes, so expected downtime is about 315.9 minutes, more than five hours, almost all of it from the single power feed. Spending more on routers would barely move the result; a second feed would. Shared causes such as one power strip feeding both routers break the independence assumption and must be designed away.

weeks.title: 95th-percentile billing — the bursts you do not pay for
weeks.lesson: NIF-5909, the second NO_AI week, is a disputed transit invoice. Many internet transit contracts bill on the 95th percentile: the provider records average throughput every five minutes, sorts the month's samples, throws away the top five percent, and bills the highest remaining sample. The course fixture has twenty samples between 289 and 905 Mbit/s. With twenty samples, five percent is one, so the bill uses the sample at sorted index ceil(0.95 × 20) − 1, which is index 18 counting from zero. Sorted, that is 720 Mbit/s, while the 905 Mbit/s burst at the top is discarded. At $0.35 per Mbit/s the charge is $252. Billing the peak would charge $316.75, and billing the mean would undercount the busy hours. A real month has about 8,640 samples, so roughly 432 five-minute periods, about 36 hours, can burst without raising the bill. Know where your provider samples, whether inbound and outbound are compared, and check their arithmetic before paying.

weeks.title: Backbone design packet — documentation numbers, recomputed
weeks.lesson: NIF-5A10 closes the term with a design packet for the regional backbone that the class has been building. It uses only documentation numbers: an autonomous system number from 64496 to 64511, here 64500, and an IPv6 prefix inside 2001:db8::/32, here 2001:db8:4400::/48. Using a real company's ASN or prefix in a training packet can leak into configurations and hijack someone else's traffic, so the reviewer rejects it on sight. The packet recomputes rather than restates: the 1,145 km route's propagation delay, the availability of the redundant core with its serial power feed and uplink compared with the 0.999 target, and the 6.4 dB optical margin. It cites RFC 4271, 5952, 7323, and 1034 for the behaviour it relies on. The final line says plainly that the packet is a classroom exercise and makes no claim about production peering or real customer service. Mentors pick one number at random and ask the author to derive it at the whiteboard.
